project_scope.note: Core set follows the existing oak module in the Hays Botany ID tracker; expand later rather than forcing every Central Texas oak into the first pass.
project_scope.learner_review_scope: Six original core Edwards Plateau oaks remain the core set; the current learner includes 12 additional native and nonlocal comparison entries. This genus visual guide teaches distinguishing characters across those entries without changing county-range or approval states.

priority: Is the blade bristle-tipped (red oak) or rounded/mucronate (white oak)? Check more than one mature leaf.
Leaf underside: star-shaped stellate hairs, vein-axil tufts, waxy/glaucous surface, and persistence of hairs.
Acorn cupule: shallow saucer vs goblet/funnel, depth relative to nut, and scales smooth vs tuberculate vs conspicuously fringed.
Twig thickness and hairs; terminal-bud scale margins and shape; bark texture.
Annual vs biennial acorn maturation when fruit age is known—do not infer it from a single photograph.
Landscape context: dry limestone upland, prairie/sand upland, mesic canyon, stream bottomland, or planted street tree.
Document hybrid/intermediate characters rather than forcing species-level identification from one leaf.
study_strategy.warning: Oak leaves can be plastic across juvenile water sprouts, shade branches, drought, and maturity. Hybridization also blurs oak characters. Read several mature leaves, their lower surfaces, buds, and (when present) mature acorns from the SAME tree; keep uncertain oak complexes at Quercus sp. or pair-level until diagnostic structures are available.
study_strategy.three_way_oak_memory: Lacey = BLUE + BARREL. White shin = THICKET + FLAT cup scales. Vasey = NARROW + BUMPY cup scales. Cupule texture works best with mature fruit and a 10× loupe.

quick_key.if: Subevergreen/live-oak form; narrow leathery leaves, undersides usually pale with appressed stellate hairs; slender pointed spindle-like nut and deep funnel/goblet cup when fruiting. Especially limestone mottes.
Live oak of coastal / eastern sandy sites with generally less pointed acorns; Central Texas planted or intermediate specimens are NOT reliably separable from escarpment live oak by one leaf.
Deciduous, deeply cut red-oak blade with several sharp bristle-tipped lobes; modest acorn in a comparatively deeper cup, frequently on dry limestone slopes.
Large deciduous red oak with bristle-tipped lobes; mature leaf often large with tufts in lower vein axils; broad shallow saucer-like acorn cup. Check against Texas red oak.
Deciduous limestone oak; broad blue-glaucous leaves, often rounded/notched at tip, usually 6–9 secondary-vein pairs; small barrel-like nut (often flattened ends) and moderately bumpy cup scales.
Low deciduous, often multistemmed limestone thicket; 7–11 secondary-vein pairs; broad/variable leaves; small nut in a very shallow cup with FLAT closely appressed scales (not tuberculate).

Evergreen/subevergreen narrow stiff leaves with 4–6 lateral vein pairs and 0–5 mucronate coarse teeth per side; tiny buds, dark strip-shredding bark; small shallow cup with STRONGLY regularly bumpy scales.
Frequently cross-shaped rounded lobes (but not always), thick yellowish hairy twigs, and harsh stellate-hairy undersides.
Broad duck-foot leaf, narrow at base and widened into 3–5 distal bristle-tipped lobes; dark, blocky bark.
Long chestnut-like blade with many evenly spaced teeth lacking bristles; side veins run toward those teeth; gray flaky bark.
Very broad lobed leaves with deep middle sinuses plus huge acorns with a long fringed/mossy cup rim.
Mostly unlobed variable evergreen leaves of a planted landscape oak with comparatively deep cups; no demonstrated native target-zone population.

curation_status.visual_polish_scope: genus quick key + real-photo comparison, no species range/taxonomy/approval changes

b065_study_strategy.warning: All four B065 taxa are Texas natives, but their native Texas ranges are eastern/coastal rather than the Central Texas target zone. Landscape occurrence around Austin/Hays does not make them target-zone native.

quick_split: Q. lyrata — overcup nearly encloses acorn; rounded-lobed white-oak leaf.
Q. michauxii — huge rounded-toothed leaf with gray pubescent underside; large sweet acorn.
Q. nigra — variable wedge/spatula-shaped leaf, often broad shallowly 3-lobed at tip.
Q. phellos — narrow willow-like entire leaves with a tiny bristle tip.

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Texas red oak ↔ Shumard oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Acorn cup depth and adult leaf underside before using overall tree size.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.buckleyi: Usually smaller dry-limestone-slope tree; mostly 7–9 bristle-tipped lobes; cup goblet/cup shaped often covering 1/3–1/2 nut; bud-scale tips distinctly ciliate.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.shumardii: Generally larger, often mesic-site tree; broad lobed adult leaves, tufts in underside vein axils, and a shallow saucer cup; mature buds often gray-brown.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Both can have lower vein-axil hair tufts; size, habitat, and leaf silhouette overlap, and hybrids occur. Do not diagnose from tufts alone.
critical_photo_roles: cup beside intact mature acorn in profile with ruler

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Escarpment live oak ↔ Southern live oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Mature intact acorn profile and cup scales, plus multiple leaves and range/provenance.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.fusiformis: Often acute, spindle-like or narrowly barrel-shaped nut with rather deep funnel/goblet cup; pale closely appressed stellate hairs beneath; frequent limestone mottes.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.virginiana: Typically less spindle-pointed nut and variable wider leaf; a generic landscape live oak or older broad-name record is insufficient to prove strict Q. virginiana.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Taxonomic treatment differs among sources; overlap and hybrids are real. Preserve the Q. virginiana taxon-concept/range UNRESOLVED state.
critical_photo_roles: matched mature acorn with cup profile and ruler

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Lacey oak ↔ White shin oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Growth habit + bark and adult leaf surfaces, then fruit.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.laceyi: Often small tree; typically broad, bluish/glaucous leaf with rounded or notched apex, light papery bark; acorns barrel-like.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.sinuata: Usually thicket-forming, multi-stemmed shrub on dry limestone; highly variable leaf lobing and small nut in very shallow cupule.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Leaves can overlap in shape and glaucousness; a shrubby shoot or one leaf is insufficient.

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Post oak ↔ Blackjack oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Inspect leaf-lobe tips with magnification, then twig hairs/bark.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.stellata: Rounded non-bristled lobes; leaves frequently cruciform; often thick yellowish stellate-hairy twigs and rough-hairy undersides.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.marilandica: Bristle-tipped distal broad lobes on a duck-foot/spatulate leaf; often dark blocky bark; a red oak.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: The cross-shaped post oak leaf is not universal; a few red-oak-like leaves do not prove blackjack.

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Chinkapin oak ↔ Bur oak ↔ Eastern swamp chestnut oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Many near-regular teeth vs deep middle sinuses vs rounded teeth; then acorn and cup.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.muehlenbergii: Narrower chestnut-like leaf, parallel veins to sharper often recurved teeth; limestone canyons/slopes; no long acorn-cup fringe.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.macrocarpa: Broad variable blade with deep midleaf waist; enormous nut, cup with conspicuous fringed rim; often alluvial limestone corridor.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.michauxii: Usually larger, more coarsely rounded teeth and densely gray-hairy underside; mainly eastern bottomland comparison.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Eastern swamp chestnut oak is a nonlocal comparison under current project rules; do not infer native occurrence from planted trees.
critical_photo_roles: matched leaves with labeled teeth and midleaf sinus

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Vasey oak ↔ Escarpment live oak
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: Margins and cup-scale texture rather than only evergreen habit.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.vaseyana: Typically 3–5 coarse mucro-tipped teeth per side; dark strip-exfoliating bark; shallow cup with strongly tuberculate scales.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.fusiformis: Leaf usually entire or only sparsely toothed; acorn spindle-like with deeper cup and thickened keeled scales, not the strongly regular tubercles of Vasey oak.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Juvenile live oak leaves may also have teeth; rely on mature branches plus fruit.

diagnostic_comparison_groups.title: Lacey oak ↔ White shin oak ↔ Vasey oak — three-way limestone key
diagnostic_comparison_groups.where_to_look_first: First decide: deciduous blue-glaucous broad leaf, deciduous thicket with flat cup scales, or narrow evergreen/subevergreen leaf with strongly bumpy cup scales. Confirm with adult leaves, twigs, buds, and a ripe cup.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.laceyi: Deciduous broad blue-green/glaucous leaf usually 40–90 × 30–60 mm; 6–9 secondary veins; often 1.5–3 mm buds; barrel-like acorn 13–15 mm, 4–7 mm deep moderately tuberculate cup.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.sinuata: Usually low deciduous multi-stem thicket; leaf often 30–60 × 20–40 mm, 7–11 secondary veins; bud 2–3 mm; small acorn generally 7–12 mm with shallow cup and flattened NONtuberculate scales.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.vaseyana: Evergreen/subevergreen narrower leaf typically 20–60 × 10–20 mm, 4–6 secondary veins; bud only 1–1.5 mm; cup 3–4 mm deep and strongly regularly tuberculate; dark bark exfoliates in strips.
diagnostic_comparison_groups.caution: Lacey blue-green color and leaf lobing vary with exposure; shin underside hairiness varies by sun/shade; Vasey can have entire margins. Measurements and cup texture overlap in some individuals. Do not identify from just one leaf.
critical_photo_roles: same-scale adult leaf upper and lower comparison for all three
match cup rim and cup scales (moderate tubercles vs flat vs strong tubercles)
habitat / whole-shrub or tree specimen-context images

visual_comparison.title: Central Texas oaks: compare the structures
visual_comparison.subtitle: Start with a real photograph, then confirm the species by lobe tips, lower-surface hairs, buds or cupules. Each caption separates visible context from characters that still need a diagnostic macro.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Bristle tip → red oak; rounded or mucro tip → white oak. Then confirm the CUP: depth, fringe, or scale texture. Always check several adult leaves and the SAME tree's twigs/acorns. Edwards Plateau trio: BLUE/BARREL = Lacey; THICKET/FLAT-SCALED CUP = white shin; NARROW/BUMPY-SCALED CUP = Vasey.

items.label: Texas red oak — deeper cup, dry limestone
items.image_role: Existing curated oak photo; reference context (cup macro still needed)
items.caption: Adult leaves typically have 7–9 sharply bristle-tipped lobes. To distinguish Shumard reliably, obtain mature cup profiles: Texas red oak is commonly deeper-cupped and has ciliate terminal-bud scales. This reference photo is not treated as cup-depth proof.
items.creator: Linda Jo Conn

items.label: Shumard oak — larger leaf, saucer cup
items.image_role: Deeply lobed foliage and twig context
items.caption: Compare adult bristle-tipped blades, then flip them to inspect lower vein-axil tufts; both species can have some tufts. Look for the broad, shallow, saucer-like ripe acorn cup to distinguish Shumard from Texas red oak.
items.creator: DouglasGoldman

items.label: Escarpment live oak — verify pointed nut
items.image_role: Existing species reference image; mature acorn macro still required
items.caption: Subevergreen leathery leaves may show dense appressed stellate hairs below. Most helpful final test is a ripe, relatively spindle-pointed nut in a deep funnel/goblet cup. Strict southern live oak is a separate unresolved comparison in this learner.
items.creator: Donovan Moxley

items.label: Lacey oak — glaucous rounded leaves
items.image_role: Same-observation field photo; verify leaf and bark view
items.caption: Lacey oak: 6–9 side veins, rounded/retuse leaf tip, strongly blue-glaucous adult leaves; erect stellate leaf hairs shed with age. Ripe cup is 4–7 mm deep with MODERATELY raised scales, nut barrel-like. Photo is a field view, not guaranteed scale or fruit macro.
items.creator: Kane Sandoval

items.label: White shin oak — low limestone thicket
items.image_role: Existing curated species reference photo; habit/cup confirmation pending
items.caption: White shin oak: often deciduous multi-stem limestone thicket, 7–11 lateral veins per side, pale flaky bark. Sun leaves may show appressed stellate hairs; shade leaves may look smoother. Mature cupule scales are FLAT, not strongly bumpy. This image needs fruit-role verification.
items.creator: Andy Blair

items.label: Vasey oak — few teeth and bumpy cup scales
items.image_role: Existing curated species reference; tuberculate cup detail still needed
items.caption: Vasey oak: 4–6 secondary veins per side and narrow evergreen/subevergreen leaves sometimes with 3–5 coarse teeth each side, sometimes entire. Very small buds (1–1.5 mm), dark bark shredding in strips; mature cup scales strongly and regularly BUMPY. Cup-scale macro is still missing.
items.creator: Curren Frasch

items.label: Post oak — rounded lobes and hairy twig
items.image_role: Existing curated oak reference; bud/hair macro still needed
items.caption: A cross-shaped leaf is a useful shortcut, but variable. The durable separation from blackjack oak is NON-bristled rounded lobes plus stout stellate-hairy yellowish twigs.
items.creator: paddymcg

items.label: Blackjack oak — bristled duck-foot blade
items.caption: Notice a broad, top-heavy spatulate leaf with 3–5 shallow distal lobes. Inspect each lobe tip for a bristle. Mature bark often breaks into nearly black rectangular blocks, unlike post oak.
items.creator: Krzysztof Ziarnek (Kenraiz)

items.label: Chinkapin oak — chestnut-like regular teeth
items.image_role: Toothed leaves and immature acorn cups
items.caption: Repeated near-parallel veins reach marginal teeth that are sharper and often recurved, without red-oak bristles. Distinguish from east-Texas swamp chestnut oak by smaller sharper-toothed leaves, site, and undersides.
items.creator: Jim Conrad

items.label: Bur oak — huge fringed acorn cup
items.caption: The massive cup with long shaggy fringe is a powerful fruiting ID. Adult leaves often have a dramatic deep middle waist; do not confuse with the evenly-toothed chinkapin oak leaf.
items.creator: USDA NRCS

visual_comparison.overlay_note: No unverified arrows or structural claims are drawn onto photographs. Several inherited core photos are generic reference/field views and require direct photo-by-photo diagnostic verification before labelling as bud, underside, or mature acorn macros. The southern-live-oak comparison still has no image; do not silently substitute escarpment live oak imagery.
